title: Why perfect designs fail
summary: A chip can pass every check and still fail: variation, heat, aging, defects the test missed, radiation and uses nobody planned for. Ship one to a phone, a car, a data center or a satellite.

learn.plain: A chip is checked on paper as if it were perfect: typical, cool, on a steady supply, and brand new. Real chips are each a little different, run hot, age and sometimes meet a stray particle from space. So engineers add margin, test hard and add protection, and each of those costs speed, power or money.
learn.engineer: Sign-off happens at a few process, voltage and temperature corners plus aging and on-chip variation; the population tail is managed with guardbands, adaptive voltage scaling and binning. Field reliability adds test-escape ppm, early failures (Weibull, screened by burn-in and part-average testing), wear-out (BTI, HCI, electromigration, TDDB) and soft errors in FIT/Mbit, handled with ECC, lockstep or TMR and in-field monitoring.

quiz.q: Engineers check a design at typical conditions. Why do real chips still fail?
options: Real chips vary, run hot, see supply dips, age, and meet defects and radiation
quiz.why: Sign-off checks one ideal chip. The real population is spread out and lives in harsher conditions, so designers add margin, test and protection.

quiz.q: Why does burn-in help a car chip?
options: Weak chips fail in the factory instead of in the car
It removes the need for testing
quiz.why: Many hidden weak spots break early in life. Running every chip hot for hours brings those failures forward, before the chip ships.

options: Stops cosmic rays from reaching the chip
Finds and fixes flipped bits using a few extra stored bits
quiz.why: Radiation cannot be stopped at ground level, but a few extra bits per word let the memory detect and correct a single flipped bit.
